## Overview

In this graded assignment, you will practice with Unix shell commands,
especially the "data tools" commands, and with Git commands.

## Directions and grading

### Submission expectations

- **Deadline**: [Sunday September 27^th^ at 11:59 pm]{style="background-color: #faf678;"}.
- **Submission**:
  Same as for GA1.
  That is, you don't need to submit anything or notify the instructors:
  we will look for files, which you'll create as part of the assignment,
  in the appropriate location at OSC.
  (We can also see when the files were last modified.)

### Academic integrity

### Rubric

You can earn a maximum of **0.5 points** for each of the 20 numbered questions/items below.

There are two **bonus** questions (21 and 22) that can also earn you 0.5 points
each, but only in case you dropped points elsewhere.

## Detailed steps

### General

- Execute Unix shell and Git commands to answer all questions unless explicitly
  instructed otherwise.

- When you issue a command in the terminal, include the command
  in a Markdown code block, and the command's output in another code block ---
  same as you did for [GA1](/GA/GA1.qmd).
  However, this isn't needed for some Git commands,
  because we can check what you did by looking at your repository,
  and because you're also allowed to use VS Code functionality instead of commands.

  To avoid confusion and make life easier for you,
  we provide you with a **template Markdown file** where you can add your answers
  (see question 1), which contains code blocks wherever needed.

  ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
  ### A worked example of how to answer a question when you ran a command _(Click to expand)_

  **Assignment questions:**

  1. Print your current working directory to screen.

  **Your answers as part of your Markdown document:**

  ````bash-in-nocolor
  ### 1: Print your current working directory to screen

  ```bash
  pwd
  ```

  The output of the command was:

  ```
  /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/jelmer
  ```
  ````
  <hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />
  :::

- Keep a **Markdown preview** open to the side while you work,
  like you did for [GA1](/GA/GA1.qmd),
  so you can check that your answers render as you intended ---
  especially the code blocks.

### Setting up

- Start a VS Code (Code Server) session at OSC OnDemand as per usual,
  and open a terminal in that session.

- Create a new dir for this assignment, `/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER/GA2`,
  and navigate there. **This will be your working dir for the entire assignment.**

### Part A: Starting a Git repository

01. Copy the **template file** for this assignment,
    `/fs/ess/PAS3493/share/GA2/GA2_template.md`, into your working dir as
    `README.md`.
    Open it in the VS Code editor and modify its title (level 1 header) to
    include **your name**.

    _You'll use this file throughout the assignment to add your answers_
    _(remove the instructional comments inside the file as you go:_
    _these are Markdown comments, i.e. text between `<!--` and `-->`,_
    _which is hidden in the Markdown preview)._

02. Initialize a Git repository inside your new directory.

03. Add & stage and then commit the README file with an appropriate commit message.

### Part B: Exploring the GTF file with Unix data tools

04. Create a dir `data` and a dir `results` inside your working dir.
    Then, copy the genome annotation GTF file `annot.gtf.gz` that is in your
    copy of the @garrigós2025 data into your `data` dir, keeping the same file name.

05. Check the file size of `annot.gtf.gz`.

06. Decompress the GTF file with the `gunzip` command below,
    and check the size of the resulting `annot.gtf` file.
    Roughly how many times larger is the uncompressed file than the compressed file?

    ```bash
    gunzip data/annot.gtf.gz
    ```

07. A GTF file starts with a few "header lines" (metadata),
    followed by its main/table section, in which each line describes one
    "genomic feature" (a gene, exon, etc.).
    Use a command to count the total number of lines in `annot.gtf`.

08. Now, look at the GTF file contents to count the number of header lines by eye,
    like in last week's exercises. How many lines does that leave for the table section?

09. Now, count the number of lines in the table section in a more automated way:
    based on what you know about what GTF header lines look like,
    combine `grep -v` with another option or command to count the number of
    lines that are not header lines. What count do you get?

    <details><summary> {{< fa lightbulb >}} _Click here for some hints._</summary>

    - The `-v` option inverts `grep`'s behavior, so that it prints all lines that do
      **not** match the pattern (see the "Additional useful `grep` options" box in
      [the section on `grep`](../week04/w4c_shell-files2.qmd#grep-to-print-lines-that-match-a-pattern)).
      Use this option with a search pattern that matches the header lines.

    - Then, to get a line count, add another `grep` option to your command,
      or pipe the output of the `grep` command into `wc -l`.

    - You should encounter a minor difference in the number of lines counted in
      this question vs. the previous one.
      If you want to, you can try to figure out why that is as part of the
      bonus question at the end.
    </details>

10. How many distinct "sequences" (chromosomes/scaffolds/contigs) are represented
    in the annotation file?
    Store a list of these distinct sequences in a file `results/scaffolds.txt`.

    <details><summary> {{< fa lightbulb >}} _Click here for some context and a hint._</summary>

    - Context: The number of sequences gives a rough idea of the quality of the
      genome assembly, because a high-quality assembly will have only a few sequences,
      ideally one per chromosome.
      (Note, though, that any sequences in the genome assembly FASTA file
      that don't have any annotated features would not be represented in the GTF file.)

    - Hint: In this and the following GTF questions, you'll only want to consider
      the table part of the file, so start your commands with the same (or a similar)
      `grep -v` command as above.
    </details>

11. Print a
    ["frequency table"](../week04/w4c_shell-files2.qmd#combining-cut-sort-and-uniq-to-create-a-list)
    of feature types in the annotation:
    this should have a count of the number of times each feature type occurs.

    <details><summary> {{< fa lightbulb >}} _Click here for some context and a hint._</summary>

    - Context: A frequency table of feature types will for example show how many
      genes have been annotated in this genome --- that's quite useful!
    - Hint: Feature types are in the 3^rd^ column of the table part of the GTF file.
    </details>

12. A labmate wants to know how many genes have been annotated in this genome,
    and runs the command below:

    ```bash
    grep -c "gene" data/annot.gtf
    ```

    Before running it, predict which of the following statements is true:

    a) This gives the correct number of genes.
    b) This overcounts the number of genes, because the word "gene" also occurs
       in lines for other feature types.
    c) This undercounts the number of genes, because `grep` only matches whole words.
    d) This command gives an error, because the file is tab-delimited.

    Then, run the command and compare its output with the number of genes
    in your frequency table from question 11.
    Was your prediction correct, and what does this comparison tell you?
    _(No points will be subtracted if you didn't predict correctly.)_

### Part C: Updating your Git repository

13. Check the status of your Git repository.
    You should see that your `README.md` has changed but also that Git has detected
    the files in the `data` and `results` dirs.

14. You don't want to commit any files in the `data` and `results` dirs,
    so create a `.gitignore` file that makes Git ignore them.
    Check the status of your repository again ---
    is your `.gitignore` file working as intended?

15. Stage and commit the `.gitignore` file.
    Then, in a separate commit, stage and commit the `README.md` file again.

### Part D: Exploring the FASTQ files with Unix data tools

16. Copy the FASTQ file `S63_R1.fastq.gz` of the @garrigós2025 data
    into your `data` dir, keeping the original file name.

17. Check the status of your Git repository. Does the FASTQ file show up? Why/why not?

18. How many reads does the FASTQ file contain?

    <details><summary> {{< fa lightbulb >}} _Click here for hints._</summary>

    Recall from the [week 4 exercises](../week04/w4_exercises.qmd)
    that a direct line count of the compressed file will **not** give you the correct answer.
    Also, don't forget to convert the number of lines to the number of reads.
    </details>

19. How many reads in the FASTQ file contain at least 10 consecutive `N`s
    (i.e., uncalled bases)?
    _(You can assume that stretches of `N`s do not occur in the quality score lines.)_

20. Stage and commit the `README.md` file again.

### Bonus

_(You don't need to commit your answer to these questions with Git, but you can if you want to.)_

21. In questions 8 and 9, you counted the number of lines in the table section
    of the GTF file in two different ways, but got different results.
    Can you figure out what accounts for the difference?

    <details><summary> {{< fa lightbulb >}} _Click here for some hints._</summary>

    - The file contains a line that is not a header line,
      but that also does not describe any genomic feature.

    - So the question boils down to: which line(s) other than the header
      lines contain the pattern you used with `grep` in question 9?

    - Review the "Additional useful `grep` options" box in
      [the section on `grep`](../week04/w4c_shell-files2.qmd#grep-to-print-lines-that-match-a-pattern)
      to find an option that might help you make sense of that.

    </details>

22. Name at least two concepts or commands that we have gone over in the course
    so far, but which you feel you do not (fully) understand.
    It helps to be specific about what you struggle with.

## Solutions

The commands below assume that your working dir is `/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/<user>/GA2`
and that your copy of the @garrigós2025 data is in `/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/<user>/garrigos`.
In the example output, `<user>` stands for your user name,
and file dates, commit IDs, etc. will differ from yours.

### Part A: Starting a Git repository

<details><summary>**1.** Copy the template file and add your name.</summary>

```bash
cp /fs/ess/PAS3493/share/GA2/GA2_template.md README.md
```

Then, in the VS Code editor,
change the level 1 header at the top of `README.md` to something like:

```markdown
# GA2 answers - Jane Doe
```

</details>

<details><summary>**2.** Initialize a Git repository.</summary>

```bash
git init
```
```bash-out
Initialized empty Git repository in /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/<user>/GA2/.git/
```

</details>

<details><summary>**3.** Stage and commit the README file.</summary>

```bash
git add README.md
git commit -m "Add README"
```

- Any commit message that describes the change is fine.
- You could also have done this with the VS Code Source Control panel.

</details>

### Part B: Exploring the GTF file with Unix data tools

<details><summary>**4.** Create `data` and `results` dirs and copy the GTF file.</summary>

```bash
mkdir data results
cp ../garrigos/ref/annot.gtf.gz data/
```

Neither command prints any output.
Using the absolute path to the GTF file
(`/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/<user>/garrigos/ref/annot.gtf.gz`) is fine too.

</details>

<details><summary>**5.** Check the file size of `annot.gtf.gz`.</summary>

```bash
ls -lh data/annot.gtf.gz
```
```bash-out
-rw-r--r-- 1 <user> PAS3493 5.1M Sep 25 14:02 data/annot.gtf.gz
```

The compressed file is **5.1 MB**.

</details>

<details><summary>**6.** Decompress the GTF file and compare file sizes.</summary>

```bash
gunzip data/annot.gtf.gz
ls -lh data/annot.gtf
```
```bash-out
-rw-r--r-- 1 <user> PAS3493 123M Sep 25 14:02 data/annot.gtf
```

The uncompressed file is 123 MB, which is roughly **24 times larger**
than the compressed file (123 / 5.1 ≈ 24).
That's a big difference, and the reason that large genomic files are typically
stored in compressed form.

</details>

<details><summary>**7.** Count the total number of lines in `annot.gtf`.</summary>

```bash
wc -l data/annot.gtf
```
```bash-out
408402 data/annot.gtf
```

The file has **408,402** lines in total.

</details>

<details><summary>**8.** Count the header lines by eye.</summary>

```bash
head -n 5 data/annot.gtf
```
```bash-out
#gtf-version 2.2
#!genome-build TS_CPP_V2
#!genome-build-accession NCBI_Assembly:GCF_016801865.2
#!annotation-source NCBI RefSeq GCF_016801865.2-RS_2022_12
NC_068937.1     Gnomon  gene    2046    110808  .       +       .       gene_id "LOC120427725"; transcript_id ""; db_xref "GeneID:120427725"; description "homeotic protein deformed"; gbkey "Gene"; gene "LOC120427725"; gene_biotype "protein_coding";
```

- There are **4** header lines, all starting with a `#`.
- That leaves 408,402 - 4 = **408,398** lines for the table section.
- Other commands to view the file, like `less -S data/annot.gtf`, are fine too.

</details>

<details><summary>**9.** Count the number of lines in the table section with `grep -v`.</summary>

```bash
grep -v "#" data/annot.gtf | wc -l
```
```bash-out
408397
```

- This gives **408,397** lines: one less than in the previous question ---
  see bonus question 21 for the explanation.
- Instead of piping to `wc -l`, you can use `grep`'s `-c` option:
  `grep -vc "#" data/annot.gtf`.
- The quotes around `#` are needed:
  without them, the shell interprets everything from the `#` onwards as a comment,
  so `grep` wouldn't get a search pattern at all.

</details>

<details><summary>**10.** Count the distinct sequences and save them to `results/scaffolds.txt`.</summary>

- First, exclude the header lines with `grep -v`.
- Then, select the first column, which contains the sequence names, with `cut -f 1`.
- To only keep distinct sequences, use `sort | uniq`, and write the output to a file.
- Finally, count the number of lines in the resulting file with `wc -l`.

```bash
grep -v "#" data/annot.gtf | cut -f 1 | sort | uniq > results/scaffolds.txt
wc -l results/scaffolds.txt
```
```bash-out
167 results/scaffolds.txt
```

- There are **167** distinct sequences.
- If you forgot `grep -v "#"`, you got 172:
  the `#` lines don't contain any tabs, so `cut` prints them in full,
  and each of these 5 lines is counted as an additional "sequence".
- The file `results/scaffolds.txt` should start like this:

  ```bash
  head -n 4 results/scaffolds.txt
  ```
  ```bash-out
  NC_015079.1
  NC_068937.1
  NC_068938.1
  NC_068939.1
  ```

</details>

<details><summary>**11.** Print a frequency table of feature types.</summary>

The feature types are in the 3^rd^ column:

```bash
grep -v "#" data/annot.gtf | cut -f 3 | sort | uniq -c
```
```bash-out
 141444 CDS
 166177 exon
  19673 gene
  25864 start_codon
  25892 stop_codon
  29347 transcript
```

- So, for example, **19,673** genes have been annotated in this genome.
- Adding `| sort -nr` to sort the table by count is a nice touch.

</details>

<details><summary>**12.** Predict, then run `grep -c "gene"`.</summary>

```bash
grep -c "gene" data/annot.gtf
```
```bash-out
408397
```

- The correct answer is **b)**: this overcounts the number of genes.
  The command returns 408,397, which is far more than the 19,673 genes in the
  frequency table from question 11.
- That's because nearly every line in the GTF file contains "gene"
  in its 9^th^ (attributes) column, in `gene_id "..."` and `gene "LOC..."`.
  In fact, 408,397 is exactly the number of table lines from question 9:
  _every_ line in the table section matches.
- The lesson: `grep` matches a pattern anywhere in a line,
  so to count genes, you need to check the feature type column specifically,
  as you did in question 11.
- Regarding the other answers:
  `grep` does _not_ only match whole words (unless you use its `-w` option),
  and it doesn't care whether a file is tab-delimited.

</details>

### Part C: Updating your Git repository

<details><summary>**13.** Check the status of your Git repository.</summary>

```bash
git status
```
```bash-out
On branch main
Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
        modified:   README.md

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
        data/
        results/

no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a")
```

`README.md` has been modified since you committed it,
and `data/` and `results/` are listed as untracked.

</details>

<details><summary>**14.** Create a `.gitignore` file and check the status again.</summary>

```bash
echo "data/" > .gitignore
echo "results/" >> .gitignore
git status
```
```bash-out
On branch main
Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
        modified:   README.md

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
        .gitignore

no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a")
```

- **Yes**, the `.gitignore` file is working:
  `data/` and `results/` are no longer listed.
  Instead, the new `.gitignore` file itself shows up as untracked.
- Creating the `.gitignore` file in the VS Code editor is fine too.
  Patterns like `data` and `results`, or `data/*` and `results/*`, also work.

</details>

<details><summary>**15.** Commit `.gitignore` and then `README.md` in separate commits.</summary>

```bash
git add .gitignore
git commit -m "Add .gitignore"

git add README.md
git commit -m "Add answers for Part B"
```

You can check that these are two separate commits with `git log`.

</details>

### Part D: Exploring the FASTQ files with Unix data tools

<details><summary>**16.** Copy the FASTQ file.</summary>

```bash
cp ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz data/
```

This command doesn't print any output.

</details>

<details><summary>**17.** Does the FASTQ file show up in `git status`?</summary>

```bash
git status
```
```bash-out
On branch main
Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
        modified:   README.md

no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a")
```

- **No**, the FASTQ file doesn't show up,
  because it is in the `data` dir, which is listed in `.gitignore`.
- Whether `README.md` is listed as modified depends on whether you had already
  added answers to it after your last commit.
  If not, you'd see "nothing to commit, working tree clean".

</details>

<details><summary>**18.** How many reads does the FASTQ file contain?</summary>

```bash
zcat data/S63_R1.fastq.gz | wc -l
```
```bash-out
2000000
```

- Each read takes up 4 lines in a FASTQ file,
  so the file contains 2,000,000 / 4 = **500,000 reads**.
- Running `wc -l data/S63_R1.fastq.gz` directly on the compressed file
  returns 101,139, which is meaningless:
  you need to count the lines of the decompressed output.

</details>

<details><summary>**19.** How many reads contain at least 10 consecutive `N`s?</summary>

```bash
zcat data/S63_R1.fastq.gz | grep -c "NNNNNNNNNN"
```
```bash-out
32612
```

- **32,612** reads contain at least 10 consecutive `N`s.
- A read with more than 10 consecutive `N`s also matches,
  and is still counted only once, since `grep -c` counts matching _lines_.

</details>

<details><summary>**20.** Stage and commit the README file again.</summary>

```bash
git add README.md
git commit -m "Add answers for Parts C and D"
```

</details>

### Bonus

<details><summary>**21.** Why do the counts from questions 8 and 9 differ?</summary>

Use `grep`'s `-n` option to print line numbers along with each matching line:

```bash
grep -n "#" data/annot.gtf
```
```bash-out
1:#gtf-version 2.2
2:#!genome-build TS_CPP_V2
3:#!genome-build-accession NCBI_Assembly:GCF_016801865.2
4:#!annotation-source NCBI RefSeq GCF_016801865.2-RS_2022_12
408402:###
```

- Besides the 4 header lines, the **last line of the file**, `###`,
  also contains a `#`.
  This line seems to function as an end-of-file marker.
- It is not a header line, so you didn't count it as one in question 8,
  but `grep -v "#"` _did_ exclude it in question 9:
  408,402 - 5 = 408,397.
- You could also have found this line by looking at the end of the file
  with `tail data/annot.gtf`.

</details>

<details><summary>**22.** Concepts or commands you don't (fully) understand.</summary>

There is no single correct answer here.

</details>
